content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) refers to an infection that can affect any part of the urinary system, including the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra. The infection is typically caused by the invasion of bacteria, viruses, fungi, or other pathogens, with bacterial infections being the most common etiology. UTIs are classified based on the anatomical site of infection into upper and lower UTIs. Lower UTIs include urethritis, prostatitis, asymptomatic bacteriuria, and cystitis (bladder infection), while upper UTIs primarily involve pyelonephritis (kidney infection) and, less commonly, ureteritis (infection of the ureters). Each subtype of UTI can be further categorized based on duration, etiology, or therapeutic approach into acute, chronic, or recurrent infections, as well as uncomplicated or complicated infections. Normally, urine is sterile, and a UTI occurs when this sterility is disrupted by bacterial invasion, leading to irritation and inflammation of the urinary tract. Pyelonephritis and cystitis are often caused by ascending infections from the urethra (urethritis) but may also result from descending infections, such as hematogenous spread or lymphatic dissemination. UTIs are more prevalent in women but can affect individuals of any gender and age group. The pathogenesis of complicated UTIs often involves factors such as urinary obstruction or stasis. Several risk factors are associated with the development of UTIs, including urinary catheter placement in hospital settings, diabetes, Crohn's disease, iatrogenic causes, endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, urinary obstruction, and bladder incontinence. A thorough physical examination is crucial for distinguishing between upper and lower UTIs. Patients with uncomplicated UTIs typically appear well, while symptoms may include abnormal urine color (cloudy), hematuria (blood in the urine), frequent or urgent urination, dysuria (painful urination), pressure in the lower pelvis or back, suprapubic pain, flank pain, back pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and chills. Laboratory tests such as urinalysis and urine culture are essential for diagnosing UTIs. Findings on urinalysis may include pyuria (presence of pus in the urine) and the presence of white blood cells (WBCs) or red blood cells (RBCs). Escherichia coli (E. coli), a bacterium commonly found in the lower gastrointestinal tract, is the most frequent causative agent of UTIs. It is important to differentiate UTIs from other causes of dysuria, such as cystitis, acute pyelonephritis, urethritis, prostatitis, vulvovaginitis, urethral strictures or diverticula, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and neoplasms such as renal cell carcinoma or cancers of the bladder, prostate, and penis. Antimicrobial therapy is indicated for symptomatic UTIs. However, a significant proportion of patients with acute uncomplicated UTIs may recover spontaneously within a few days or weeks without treatment. If left untreated, some patients may develop recurrent infections, spread of the infection to other parts of the urinary tract, hematuria, or, in rare cases, renal failure. The prognosis for lower UTIs is generally favorable. The treatment of UTIs depends on the type of infection, the disease course (acute uncomplicated versus complicated), the patient’s medical history, and local rates of antimicrobial resistance. Preventative measures to reduce the risk of UTIs include abstinence, monogamy, condom use, barrier contraception during sexual intercourse, urinating after intercourse, increasing fluid intake and frequency of urination, and the use of estrogen in postmenopausal women. UTIs can be classified anatomically or based on symptoms, which helps guide the duration of antibiotic treatment. The most common cause of UTIs across all types is E. coli. Differential diagnosis is essential to distinguish UTIs from other diseases. Treatment strategies vary depending on the specific type of UTI, and detailed treatment guidelines are available for conditions such as asymptomatic bacteriuria, cystitis, urethritis, prostatitis, and pyelonephritis.
